summary:
Public Law 118-186, the "Detection Equipment and Technology Evaluation to Counter the Threat of Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024" (or "DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024"), enacted December 23, 2024, requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Science and Technology Directorate to develop greater capacity to detect and identify illicit substances in very low concentrations.

Section 2 amends Section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 182) by adding a new paragraph (15). This provision authorizes the Directorate, in coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), to conduct research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses to improve the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of equipment and reference libraries used by Federal, State, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies for the accurate detection of drugs such as fentanyl and xylazine. Specifically, the new authority covers: (A) portable equipment capable of detecting and identifying drugs with minimal or no sample handling; (B) equipment that separates complex mixtures containing low concentrations of drugs and high concentrations of cutting agents into component parts to enable signature extraction for field identification; and (C) technologies utilizing machine learning or artificial intelligence, as defined in Section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401), to predict whether sample substances are controlled substance analogues or other new psychoactive substances not yet included in available reference libraries.

Section 3 imposes administrative requirements on the Under Secretary for Science and Technology in carrying out the new 6 U.S.C. 182(15). The Under Secretary must follow the recommendations, guidelines, and best practices described in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) or any successor document. Additionally, the Under Secretary must establish the Directorate's research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis priorities based on the latest available information, including specific drugs identified as threats in the latest DHS Homeland Threat Assessment, the latest DEA State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or any successor documents.

Section 4 provides a rule of construction, stipulating that nothing in the Act may be construed to limit the authority of agencies currently managing, overseeing, or otherwise involved in drug equipment and reference libraries. The Act contains no explicit authorizations of appropriations or direct appropriations.
